title: CTS The Doctrine of Sin — Unit 6

blocks.en: 📖 Systematic Theology — Unit 6: The Doctrine of Sin
blocks.es_reference: 📖 Teología Sistemática — Unidad 6: La Doctrina del Pecado

blocks.en: Professor: Dr. Wayne Cook | Director: Dr. Ted Rogers
blocks.es_reference: Profesor: Dr. Wayne Cook | Director: Dr. Ted Rogers

blocks.en: "All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God." — Romans 3:23 (NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: "Por cuanto todos pecaron, y están destituidos de la gloria de Dios." — Romanos 3:23 (RVG)

blocks.en: Day 1 — The Reality and Seriousness of Sin
blocks.es_reference: Día 1 — La Realidad y Seriedad del Pecado

blocks.en: Sin is one of the most important and least popular subjects in theology. Many people prefer to speak only of love, grace, and forgiveness. These are essential truths, but without a clear understanding of sin, they lose their meaning. Grace only makes sense when we understand what we are being saved from.
blocks.es_reference: El pecado es uno de los temas más importantes y menos populares en la teología. Muchas personas prefieren hablar solo de amor, gracia y perdón. Estas son verdades esenciales, pero sin una comprensión clara del pecado, pierden su significado. La gracia solo tiene sentido cuando entendemos de qué estamos siendo salvos.

blocks.en: The Bible does not treat sin lightly. It presents sin as rebellion against God, a violation of His holy law, and a distortion of what humanity was created to be. Sin is not merely a mistake or a weakness. It is a moral failure rooted in the human heart.
blocks.es_reference: La Biblia no trata el pecado a la ligera. Presenta el pecado como rebelión contra Dios, una violación de Su santa ley y una distorsión de lo que la humanidad fue creada para ser. El pecado no es meramente un error o una debilidad. Es un fracaso moral arraigado en el corazón humano.

blocks.en: In modern culture, sin is often redefined or avoided. We speak of mistakes, dysfunction, or poor choices rather than moral responsibility. Yet Scripture speaks clearly. Sin is real, and it is serious.
blocks.es_reference: En la cultura moderna, el pecado a menudo se redefine o se evita. Hablamos de errores, disfunción o malas decisiones en lugar de responsabilidad moral. Sin embargo, la Escritura habla con claridad. El pecado es real, y es serio.

blocks.en: Sin separates us from God. It disrupts our relationship with Him and introduces disorder into every part of life. The holiness of God makes sin not just unfortunate, but offensive.
blocks.es_reference: El pecado nos separa de Dios. Interrumpe nuestra relación con Él e introduce desorden en cada parte de la vida. La santidad de Dios hace que el pecado no sea solo desafortunado, sino ofensivo.

blocks.en: Understanding sin is essential for understanding salvation. If sin is minimized, then the cross of Christ becomes unnecessary. But when sin is seen clearly, the cross becomes central.
blocks.es_reference: Entender el pecado es esencial para entender la salvación. Si el pecado se minimiza, entonces la cruz de Cristo se vuelve innecesaria. Pero cuando el pecado se ve con claridad, la cruz se vuelve central.

blocks.en: "For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God." — Romans 3:23
blocks.es_reference: "Por cuanto todos pecaron, y están destituidos de la gloria de Dios." — Romanos 3:23

blocks.en: "The wages of sin is death." — Romans 6:23
blocks.es_reference: "La paga del pecado es muerte." — Romanos 6:23

blocks.en: When we avoid the doctrine of sin, we do not make people better — we leave them without a solution.
blocks.es_reference: Cuando evitamos la doctrina del pecado, no hacemos mejores a las personas — las dejamos sin una solución.

blocks.en: Day 2 — The Origin and Nature of Sin
blocks.es_reference: Día 2 — El Origen y la Naturaleza del Pecado

blocks.en: Sin entered the human race through Adam's disobedience in the Garden of Eden. The first sin was not murder or theft—it was disbelief in God's word and the choice to act independently of His command. Adam and Eve had one prohibition, and they violated it. They chose their own judgment over God's revelation.
blocks.es_reference: El pecado entró en la raza humana a través de la desobediencia de Adán en el Jardín del Edén. El primer pecado no fue asesinato ni robo—fue la incredulidad en la palabra de Dios y la decisión de actuar independientemente de Su mandato. Adán y Eva tenían una sola prohibición, y la violaron. Eligieron su propio juicio sobre la revelación de Dios.

blocks.en: Sin is both an act and a condition. It is an act when we choose to disobey God. It is a condition because we are born with a nature inclined toward sin. This is why Scripture speaks of being "dead in trespasses and sins" (Ephesians 2:1). The problem is not only what we do—it is what we are.
blocks.es_reference: El pecado es tanto un acto como una condición. Es un acto cuando elegimos desobedecer a Dios. Es una condición porque nacemos con una naturaleza inclinada hacia el pecado. Por eso la Escritura habla de estar "muertos en delitos y pecados" (Efesios 2:1). El problema no es solo lo que hacemos—es lo que somos.

blocks.en: Sin as Both Act and Condition
blocks.es_reference: El Pecado como Acto y Condición

blocks.en: If sin were only external, we could fix ourselves. But because it is internal, we need transformation. Education cannot save us. Moral reform cannot save us. Only the work of God can change the human heart.
blocks.es_reference: Si el pecado fuera solo externo, podríamos arreglarnos a nosotros mismos. Pero porque es interno, necesitamos transformación. La educación no puede salvarnos. La reforma moral no puede salvarnos. Solo la obra de Dios puede cambiar el corazón humano.

blocks.en: Examples of faith show how sin operates. The "leprous babe" illustration speaks of a baby in Jerusalem who appeared healthy but carried the germ of leprosy within. Though he looked perfect, the disease was hidden deep within his nature and would eventually manifest. This is the biblical view of original sin. We are not sinners because we sin; we sin because we carry the "germ" of a fallen nature. Jesus said it is not what goes into us that defiles us, but what comes out of the heart.
blocks.es_reference: Los ejemplos de fe muestran cómo opera el pecado. La ilustración del "bebé leproso" habla de un bebé en Jerusalén que parecía saludable pero llevaba el germen de la lepra en su interior. Aunque parecía perfecto, la enfermedad estaba escondida en lo profundo de su naturaleza y eventualmente se manifestaría. Esta es la visión bíblica del pecado original. No somos pecadores porque pecamos; pecamos porque llevamos el "germen" de una naturaleza caída. Jesús dijo que no es lo que entra en nosotros lo que nos contamina, sino lo que sale del corazón.

blocks.en: 💡 The Leprous Babe: Dr. John A. Broadus spoke of seeing a baby in Jerusalem who appeared ruddy-cheeked and healthy. Yet, as he reached over to pick the child up, he heard the startling cry, "Unclean! Unclean!" The child was the offspring of lepers. Though he looked perfect, the germ of the disease was hidden deep within his nature and would eventually manifest. We are not sinners because we sin; we sin because we carry the "germ" of a fallen nature.
blocks.es_reference: 💡 El Bebé Leproso: El Dr. John A. Broadus habló de ver a un bebé en Jerusalén que parecía sonrosado y saludable. Sin embargo, cuando se acercó para recoger al niño, escuchó el grito alarmante: "¡Inmundo! ¡Inmundo!" El niño era hijo de leprosos. Aunque parecía perfecto, el germen de la enfermedad estaba escondido en lo profundo de su naturaleza y eventualmente se manifestaría. No somos pecadores porque pecamos; pecamos porque llevamos el "germen" de una naturaleza caída.

blocks.en: Day 3 — The Linguistic Anatomy of Failure: Hamartia
blocks.es_reference: Día 3 — La Anatomía Lingüística del Fracaso: Hamartia

blocks.en: The primary biblical concept for sin is Hamartia — a term from archery. It describes the archer who aims at the target of God's glory and misses. Crucially, in this theological sense, the archer doesn't just hit the outer ring; he misses the target entirely. He fails to hit the mark of God's perfect will. As Romans 3:23 states, we have all "fallen short." This "missing" is often intentional (rebellion) or through wandering (ignorance), but the result is always a chasm between our performance and God's standard.
blocks.es_reference: El concepto bíblico principal para el pecado es Hamartia — un término del tiro con arco. Describe al arquero que apunta al blanco de la gloria de Dios y falla. Crucialmente, en este sentido teológico, el arquero no solo toca el anillo exterior; falla el blanco por completo. No alcanza el estándar de la voluntad perfecta de Dios. Como Romanos 3:23 declara, todos hemos sido "destituidos". Este "fallar" es a menudo intencional (rebelión) o por vagar (ignorancia), pero el resultado es siempre un abismo entre nuestro desempeño y el estándar de Dios.

blocks.en: Sin is also described in Scripture using other terms. It is called transgression — the crossing of a boundary. It is called iniquity — a twisting or perversion of what is right. It is called debt — something owed to God that we cannot pay. Each term adds depth to our understanding. Sin is not a single thing but a multifaceted reality. Yet at its core, sin is always a failure to be what God created us to be and to do what God commands us to do.
blocks.es_reference: El pecado también se describe en la Escritura usando otros términos. Se llama transgresión — el cruce de un límite. Se llama iniquidad — un torcimiento o perversión de lo que es correcto. Se llama deuda — algo debido a Dios que no podemos pagar. Cada término añade profundidad a nuestra comprensión. El pecado no es una sola cosa sino una realidad multifacética. Sin embargo, en su esencia, el pecado es siempre un fracaso de ser lo que Dios nos creó para ser y de hacer lo que Dios nos manda hacer.

blocks.en: Day 4 — The Perversion of the Positive and Sins of Commission/Omission
blocks.es_reference: Día 4 — La Perversión de lo Positivo y los Pecados de Comisión y Omisión

blocks.en: One of the most creative ways to understand sin is as the "abuse of the positive." Most of our natural desires are gifts from God, but they can all be abused or misdirected. Alcohol can propel a car as fuel, or it can be abused to propel a person drunkenly into the street. Water can quench a life-threatening thirst, or it can be used to drown someone. Sex is a holy gift for intimacy and family, yet it is abused through promiscuity, adultery, and lust. Fire warms the hearth or consumes the city. Sin is the act of taking a "good" desire and aiming it toward an abusive end. The desire for food becomes gluttony; the desire for rest becomes laziness.
blocks.es_reference: Una de las maneras más creativas de entender el pecado es como el "abuso de lo positivo". La mayoría de nuestros deseos naturales son dones de Dios, pero todos pueden ser abusados o mal dirigidos. El alcohol puede impulsar un automóvil como combustible, o puede ser abusado para impulsar a una persona ebria a la calle. El agua puede saciar una sed peligrosa, o puede usarse para ahogar a alguien. El sexo es un don santo para la intimidad y la familia, sin embargo se abusa a través de la promiscuidad, el adulterio y la lujuria. El fuego calienta el hogar o consume la ciudad. El pecado es el acto de tomar un deseo "bueno" y dirigirlo hacia un fin abusivo. El deseo de comida se convierte en glotonería; el deseo de descanso se convierte en pereza.

blocks.en: Sin also manifests in our daily conduct in two distinct ways:
blocks.es_reference: El pecado también se manifiesta en nuestra conducta diaria de dos maneras distintas:

blocks.en: Sins of Commission: These are the "active rebellions." We see God's "No" and we do it anyway. We willfully fire our "arrow" in the opposite direction of the target.
blocks.es_reference: Pecados de Comisión: Son las "rebeliones activas". Vemos el "No" de Dios y lo hacemos de todos modos. Disparamos voluntariamente nuestra "flecha" en dirección opuesta al blanco.

blocks.en: Sins of Omission
blocks.es_reference: Pecados de Omisión

blocks.en: Sins of Omission: These are the "passive failures." We know the good we should do, but we fail to do it. As James 4:17 states, to know the good and fail to do it is sin. We miss the mark through our silence and our inaction.
blocks.es_reference: Pecados de Omisión: Son los "fracasos pasivos". Sabemos el bien que debemos hacer, pero no lo hacemos. Como declara Santiago 4:17, saber el bien y no hacerlo es pecado. Fallamos el blanco a través de nuestro silencio y nuestra inacción.

blocks.en: "Therefore, to him who knows to do good and does not do it, to him it is sin." — James 4:17
blocks.es_reference: "Al que sabe hacer lo bueno y no lo hace, le es pecado." — Santiago 4:17

blocks.en: 💡 The Alcohol-Logic: Both the man who uses alcohol to fuel his car and the man who uses alcohol to fuel his drunkenness are using the same substance. The difference is not in the thing itself, but in the direction of the use. Sin is not the destruction of the good; it is the misdirection of the good.
blocks.es_reference: 💡 La Lógica del Alcohol: Tanto el hombre que usa alcohol para alimentar su automóvil como el que usa alcohol para alimentar su embriaguez están usando la misma sustancia. La diferencia no está en la cosa misma, sino en la dirección del uso. El pecado no es la destrucción de lo bueno; es la mala dirección de lo bueno.

blocks.en: Day 5 — The Great Distinction: Sin versus Sins
blocks.es_reference: Día 5 — La Gran Distinción: Pecado vs. Pecados

blocks.en: To master this doctrine, one must distinguish between Sin (the nature) and Sins (the actions).
blocks.es_reference: Para dominar esta doctrina, uno debe distinguir entre Pecado (la naturaleza) y Pecados (las acciones).

blocks.en: Sin (The Condition): This refers to the corrupted state of the human race. No one person seems responsible for it, yet things are in a terrible state. As a result of this condition, we find "problems without individual responsibility"—diseases, wars, earthquakes, and floods. This is the "helpless" state described in Romans 5-7. As theologian Fisher Humphreys famously noted: "In our sin we are helpless and need liberation."
blocks.es_reference: Pecado (La Condición): Se refiere al estado corrupto de la raza humana. Ninguna persona parece responsable de él, sin embargo las cosas están en un estado terrible. Como resultado de esta condición, encontramos "problemas sin responsabilidad individual" — enfermedades, guerras, terremotos e inundaciones. Este es el estado "indefenso" descrito en Romanos 5-7. Como notó famosamente el teólogo Fisher Humphreys: "En nuestro pecado somos indefensos y necesitamos liberación".

blocks.en: Sins (The Transgressions): These are the result of our freedom of choice. These are the specific, willful decisions we make that run contrary to God's will, as cataloged in Romans 1-3. For these, we are personally guilty and need forgiveness.
blocks.es_reference: Pecados (Las Transgresiones): Son el resultado de nuestra libertad de elección. Son las decisiones específicas y voluntarias que tomamos que van en contra de la voluntad de Dios, catalogadas en Romanos 1-3. Por estos, somos personalmente culpables y necesitamos perdón.

blocks.en: One requires liberation from a state; the other requires forgiveness for an act. Addressing one without the other leads to incomplete ministry. The gospel addresses both: Christ liberates us from the power of sin and forgives us for the acts of sin.
blocks.es_reference: Uno requiere liberación de un estado; el otro requiere perdón por un acto. Abordar uno sin el otro lleva a un ministerio incompleto. El evangelio aborda ambos: Cristo nos libera del poder del pecado y nos perdona por los actos del pecado.

blocks.en: Final Summary: The Path to Liberation
blocks.es_reference: Resumen Final: El Camino a la Liberación

blocks.en: The Doctrine of Sin is never the final word. It identifies the "missed mark" so we realize that we cannot save ourselves. Instead, we need a Substitute Archer — Jesus Christ — who hit the mark perfectly and whose righteousness is credited to us by grace.
blocks.es_reference: La Doctrina del Pecado nunca es la palabra final. Identifica el "blanco fallado" para que nos demos cuenta de que no podemos salvarnos a nosotros mismos. En cambio, necesitamos un Arquero Sustituto — Jesucristo — que acertó en el blanco perfectamente y cuya justicia se nos acredita por gracia.

blocks.en: Sin is real, serious, and universal. It entered through Adam, affects every part of our being, and leads to death. But the gospel announces that where sin abounded, grace abounded much more (Romans 5:20). The diagnosis of sin prepares us for the cure of salvation. To understand sin is to understand why we need a Savior. To understand grace is to understand what we have received in Him.
blocks.es_reference: El pecado es real, serio y universal. Entró por Adán, afecta cada parte de nuestro ser y lleva a la muerte. Pero el evangelio anuncia que donde el pecado abundó, sobreabundó la gracia (Romanos 5:20). El diagnóstico del pecado nos prepara para la cura de la salvación. Entender el pecado es entender por qué necesitamos un Salvador. Entender la gracia es entender lo que hemos recibido en Él.

blocks.en: "But God demonstrates His own love toward us, in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us." — Romans 5:8
blocks.es_reference: "Mas Dios muestra su amor para con nosotros, en que siendo aún pecadores, Cristo murió por nosotros." — Romanos 5:8

mc.why: Sin is rebellion against God and violation of His holy law.
Understanding sin helps us understand why we need salvation.
Sin entered the human race through Adam's disobedience.
Sin is both an act we commit and a condition we inherit.
Total depravity means every part of human nature is affected by sin.
The noetic effects of sin mean the mind is darkened regarding spiritual truth.
The will is weakened and enslaved to selfish desires.
Emotions are disordered and prone to love what we should hate.
Sin affects the entire person — mind, will, emotions, and body.
Every sin is first and foremost an offense against God (Psalm 51:4).
The ground was cursed because of sin; all creation groans (Romans 8:22).
Sin hardens the heart, making it easier to sin again (Hebrews 3:13).
The wages of sin is death (Romans 6:23).
Sin always promises freedom but produces bondage.

fill.prompt: Sin is not merely a mistake or a weakness: the Bible presents it as ____ against God, an uprising against His rule and a violation of His holy law.

sa.prompt: Explain the distinction between sin as a nature and sins as actions. Why is this distinction important for understanding the gospel?
sa.model: The unit distinguishes sin from sins. Sins are the wrong things we do, the individual acts; sin is the deeper nature or condition we are born with, the corrupt root out of which those acts grow. This distinction matters for the gospel because if our problem were only sins, we might hope to fix ourselves by trying harder and doing better. But because the problem is a sinful nature, an inward condition we cannot cure by effort, we need more than reform; we need a new heart and new birth. The gospel addresses the root, not just the fruit. Understanding sin as nature shows why salvation must be God's transforming work and not mere moral self-improvement.

sa.prompt: What does the "Leprous Babe" illustration teach about original sin?
sa.model: The unit uses the leprous babe to teach the truth of original sin. A newborn with leprosy looks innocent and harmless, yet it already carries the disease from birth; the corruption is present long before any symptom shows. In the same way, every person is born with a sinful nature already in place, not acquired later by bad choices alone. The illustration teaches that sin is a condition we inherit, not merely a habit we pick up, and that outward innocence does not mean inward purity. This is why even those who have not yet committed obvious sins still need salvation: the nature is there from the start, and it will surely express itself in time.

sa.prompt: Explain the meaning of the Greek word "hamartia" and how it helps us understand the nature of sin.
sa.model: The unit explains that hamartia, the main Greek word for sin, means to miss the mark, like an archer whose arrow falls short of or strays from the target. This image helps us understand sin as failing to hit the standard God has set, not merely breaking arbitrary rules. Sin is falling short of the mark of God's glory and righteousness, whether by going wrong or by failing to reach what we were aimed at. The word captures both deliberate wrongdoing and simple failure to measure up. Understanding sin as missing the mark keeps us from thinking of it only as scandalous acts; it includes every way we fall short of the target God intended for human life.

sa.prompt: Explain the difference between sins of commission and sins of omission. Give an example of each.
sa.model: The unit distinguishes two kinds of sin. A sin of commission is doing what we ought not to do, an actual wrong committed, such as lying, stealing, or speaking cruelly. A sin of omission is failing to do the good we ought to do, the right action left undone, such as refusing to help someone in need or staying silent when we should speak the truth. The difference is between wrong done and good neglected. This matters because we often measure ourselves only by the obvious sins of commission, while Scripture counts the good we fail to do as real sin too. To know to do good and not do it is itself sin, so righteousness is not merely avoiding wrong but actively doing right.

sa.prompt: What does the "Alcohol-Logic" illustration teach about how sin "borrows" from the good?
sa.model: The unit uses the alcohol-logic example to teach that sin has no independent existence of its own; it always borrows from something good and twists it. Just as alcohol takes the good of grain or fruit and ferments it into something distorted, sin takes a genuine good God created and bends it out of its proper place. Sin is therefore a perversion of the positive rather than an original thing in its own right; it is a counterfeit, parasitic on the good it corrupts. This teaches that nothing God made is evil in itself, and that evil is the misuse and distortion of good. Even the worst sins are good things turned wrong, which is why sin is so deceptive: it always trades on a real good underneath.

sa.prompt: Explain the relationship between the fall of Lucifer (Isaiah 14:12-14) and the fall of humanity (Genesis 3).
sa.model: The unit links the two falls by a common root: pride and the desire to exalt the self above God. Isaiah 14:12-14 describes Lucifer's fall in his repeated "I will" statements, his determination to ascend and be like the Most High. That same temptation reappears in Genesis 3, where humanity is enticed to become like God on its own terms by disobeying His word. The fall of humanity echoes the fall of the tempter: both turn from submission to God toward self-exaltation. The relationship teaches that sin at its core is the creature's refusal to keep its rightful place under God, and that the same prideful impulse that ruined Lucifer is what the tempter used to draw humanity into the same ruin.

sa.prompt: Why can education, culture, and laws not solve the fundamental problem of sin?
sa.model: The unit teaches that education, culture, and laws all work on the outside, while sin's true seat is on the inside. These good things can inform the mind, refine behavior, and restrain conduct, but they cannot change the sinful nature of the heart. If sin were merely ignorance, education could cure it; if it were merely bad environment, culture could fix it; if it were merely lack of rules, law could solve it. But because sin is an inward condition, no external remedy reaches deep enough. People who are well-educated, cultured, and law-abiding still sin, because the problem is what they are, not only what they know or where they live. Only the new birth, a change God works within, can address the root that these external means leave untouched.

sa.prompt: Explain why, in the gospel, the doctrine of sin is "never the final word."
sa.model: The unit insists that, while sin must be taken with full seriousness, it is never where the gospel stops. The doctrine of sin is the diagnosis, not the cure; it tells us how deep the problem goes precisely so that grace can be seen as the answer. After the bad news of sin comes the good news of redemption in Christ, who deals with both the guilt of our sins and the corruption of our nature. To leave a person only with the doctrine of sin would be to leave them in despair, but the gospel moves on to grace, forgiveness, and a path to liberation. So sin is taught honestly but always as the dark background against which the light of Christ shines; the final word is grace, not condemnation.

sa.prompt: What does the "Substitute Archer" illustration teach about the work of Christ for the sinner?
sa.model: Building on sin as missing the mark, the unit uses the substitute archer to teach the work of Christ. We are the archers whose every shot falls short of God's perfect standard; we cannot hit the target no matter how hard we try. Christ steps in as the substitute archer who hits the mark perfectly in our place, doing what we could never do. His perfect righteousness is credited to us, so that our failure to hit the target is covered by His success. The illustration teaches substitution: Christ takes our place and accomplishes the perfect obedience we owe but cannot render. This is why the doctrine of sin leads to the gospel, because the One who never missed the mark stands in for those who always do.

sa.prompt: Summarize the main point of Unit 6. Why must sin be understood before grace can be appreciated?
sa.model: The main point of the unit is that sin is real, serious, and deeper than our actions, being a nature and condition as well as a set of deeds, and that no external remedy can cure it. Yet sin is never the final word, because it sets the stage for grace. Sin must be understood before grace can be appreciated for the same reason a cure means little to someone who does not know they are sick: only when we see how deep the disease goes do we treasure the remedy. A shallow view of sin produces a shallow gratitude for salvation, while an honest view of sin makes grace astonishing. So the unit teaches sin seriously precisely in order to lead the student to value the liberation and forgiveness that come in Christ.
